newsitem.title: CHINA: HK in talks with China garrison on border checks.
newsitem.headline: HK in talks with China garrison on border checks.

text.p: Hong Kong's customs department was holding discussions with the territory's Chinese garrison on how to handle troops suspected of smuggling or other offences, government radio reported on Saturday.

The former British colony remains a separate customs territory after it reverted to China on July 1, but vehicles of the People's Liberation Army (PLA) garrison here are exempt from inspection when travelling into and out of Hong Kong.

Commissioner of Customs and Excise Lawrence Li said discussions between his department and the PLA were underway to resolve the matter of PLA forces who could be suspected of smuggling or other offences, RTHK radio reported on Saturday.
The two sides were expected to carry out joint inspections of suspected vehicles at the border, he was quoted as saying.

The PLA garrison is a sensitive subject in Hong Kong, where many remember with dismay the military's role in the bloody crackdown against student-led Tiananmen democracy protesters in Beijing in 1989.
The PLA's extensive businesses in China, and its soldiers' relatively low pay in one of the world's most expensive cities, have also raised concerns of possible smuggling and corruption.

The garrison law covering the troops' duties and responsibilities not only exempts them from customs inspections, it bars Hong Kong courts from trying cases involving offences by on-duty soldiers, who can only be tried by military courts.
Offences committed by off-duty personnel can be handled by local courts in Hong Kong. The law also bars the garrison from conducting business in the territory.
Meanwhile, the Hong Kong government's newly announced guidelines allowing police to ban protests or political groups on "national security" grounds drew a mixed response.
The guidelines issued on Friday allow the police chief to ban gatherings if they threaten China's security, promote independence for Tibet or Taiwan, or cause public disturbance.
The Ming Pao Daily said the vast majority of Hong Kong people did not support independence for Taiwan or Tibet, and advocacy by a few could not threaten national unity or security.
"If the police are over-sensitive in applying the limits, that will harm Hong Kong's international image," the Chinese-language daily warned.

The English-language Hong Kong Standard said no one who accepted that China proper includes Hong Kong, Taiwan and Tibet would have any quarrel with the limits, and welcomed the tolerance for criticism of China's national leadership.

"Contrary to the declarations of mainland leaders that slogans like 'Down with (Prime Minister) Li Peng' or 'Down with the Communist Party' would be illegal, the government is emphatic that such slogans will be allowed," it said.
But the Chinese-language Apple Daily said it believed the guidelines were too general and vague, which could lead to problems.

"Three weeks since the establishment of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, the police have shown protesters a degree of respect and restraint that deserves commendation," it said. " We hope that tolerant attitude can be maintained in the future to allow society to have many voices."
